1b11db565e.e: Episode 32: The Evolution of Freight Fraud
f: Freight fraud has shifted from easily detectable phone-based schemes where a fraudster's voice or background noise gave them away, to AI-powered impersonation tactics that use stolen carrier identities and publicly available information to bypass standard vetting . Bad actors now call in posing as legitimate carriers, leveraging artificial intelligence to make their schemes far more convincing and harder to identify in real time.
The anatomy of the shift: From audio cues to digital deception

In the early days of carrier fraud detection, the vulnerabilities were acoustic. When fraudsters called booking centers to arrange shipments under false pretenses, trained ears could catch inconsistencies—a hesitant tone, unfamiliar background noise, or telltale signs that something didn't match the carrier's profile.

That tactical advantage has evaporated. As Eric Garcia explains in this episode , the modern fraudster arsenal now includes AI tools that enable more convincing imitation across multiple fronts: synthesized voices, scripted responses, and stolen carrier credentials pulled from publicly searchable databases. The information fraudsters need to sound legitimate is no longer hidden—it's freely available online.

This democratization of fraud capability means that even less sophisticated bad actors can now execute highly credible schemes. The barrier to entry has lowered, while the barrier to detection has risen sharply.

The Cascade of Weather-Driven Disruptions

Hurricane season doesn't strike a single point in your supply chain—it strikes everywhere at once. Flooded roads block routes that were available yesterday, forcing urgent rerouting decisions while your shipments are already in transit. Ports close their gates, freezing inbound and outbound cargo regardless of how much you've invested in efficient scheduling. Power outages don't just slow warehouses; they halt tracking systems, communication networks, and the visibility you depend on to make real-time decisions.

The least obvious but equally damaging challenge is shifting carrier capacity . When severe weather hits, carriers don't vanish—they redeploy to higher-priority routes, emergency relief, or simply scale back operations. Your contracted capacity shrinks without notice, and the rates for remaining availability spike. As discussed in the podcast , the right transportation partner helps you navigate these simultaneous pressures by staying ahead of capacity changes before they hit your door.

The common thread across all four disruptions is timing: they develop faster than reactive responses can address them . A flooded road becomes impassable in hours; a port closure can be announced with minimal warning; carrier networks contract in real time. By the time you're aware of the problem, your freight is already caught in it.

Why This Three-Day Window Changes Everything

DOT Blitz Week concentrates what would normally be spread across weeks into just 72 continuous hours of heightened inspection activity at weigh stations and along major highways. 3464eb9d29.q: How have spot market rates changed in the freight industry over the past six to eight months compared to historical benchmarks?
3464eb9d29.a: The fastest climb in spot market rates ever experienced in the freight market has occurred over the last six to eight months, even challenging what was experienced during early COVID days. Spot rates are now 30% to 40% higher inclusive of fuel, and 20% to 30% higher excluding fuel compared to the previous year.
3464eb9d29.e: Episode 31: 2026 Mid-Year State of the Freight
f: Spot market rates have experienced the fastest climb ever recorded in freight history over the past six to eight months , with increases of 30–40% when including fuel surcharges and 20–30% when excluding them, compared to the previous year. This surge has even exceeded the dramatic rate spikes seen during the early days of COVID.

The magnitude of this shift represents a complete reversal of market conditions. For years, the freight industry had been navigating excess capacity and favorable conditions for shippers. Then, as Brett Leifert explains in the episode , something fundamental changed around Q4 of the previous year, and the acceleration has continued unabated into mid-2026.
A Supply-Driven Market Transformation

The root cause of this unprecedented rate climb is a sharp exit of capacity from the market , far more than a surge in demand. Tens of thousands of non-domicile CDL drivers left the industry following FMCSA enforcement actions, roughly 2,000 Mexican drivers lost their ability to enter the U.S. due to cabotage enforcement, and north of 50 CDL schools closed across the southwest, Texas, and California. Each of these factors simultaneously reduced the supply side of trucking.

What makes this environment distinct is that while demand has shown early signs of recovery, the real story remains the capacity constraint. As Leifert describes it, "This is truly a supply driven recovery. Demands have some green shoots, but it's really more about the exit of capacity." This imbalance has left shippers facing spot rate pressures not seen since the early pandemic , even as overall freight volumes remain more moderate than during that earlier crisis.
"This is truly a supply driven recovery. Demands have some green shoots, but it's really more about the exit of capacity."

8a8f3e4253.q: What regulatory and enforcement changes have most significantly impacted truck driver supply in recent years?

8a8f3e4253.e: Episode 31: 2026 Mid-Year State of the Freight
f: The most significant regulatory impact came from FMCSA enforcement crackdowns on non-domicile CDLs , which caused tens of thousands of drivers to exit the market. This single factor became one of the biggest drivers of truck driver supply contraction in recent years, fundamentally reshaping capacity availability across the industry.
The COVID-Era Influx and Regulatory Reversal

During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-domicile CDLs exploded as a new entry channel for drivers entering the trucking market. Tens of thousands of drivers came through immigration pathways and entirely new avenues to obtain commercial licenses without establishing domicile in a specific state. This temporary regulatory opening provided a significant boost to driver supply during periods of acute shortage.

However, the trajectory reversed sharply once federal enforcement intensified. As detailed in this episode of Hit The Brakes , states that had been issuing non-domicile CDLs ceased doing so following FMCSA enforcement actions, creating an immediate and substantial contraction in the driver pool.
Compounding Enforcement Actions

The impact extended beyond non-domicile CDL restrictions. Roughly 2,000 Mexican drivers lost their visas to enter the U.S. due to cabotage enforcement, further reducing accessible labor supply. Simultaneously, over 50 CDL schools closed in southwest, Texas, and California regions—eliminating key pipeline infrastructure that had been training new drivers.

ace1d3c746.q: What is the connection between electronic logging device fraud and artificially inflated freight capacity?
ace1d3c746.a: Electronic logging devices, manufactured by over 100 different companies and mostly self-certified by manufacturers, have enabled fraud where drivers can artificially reset their hours-of-service status. FMCSA has been decertifying many ELD devices that were artificially allowing drivers to drive beyond legal hours of service, thereby removing artificial capacity from the market.
ace1d3c746.e: Episode 31: 2026 Mid-Year State of the Freight
f: Fraudulent electronic logging devices (ELDs), manufactured by over 100 different companies and mostly self-certified by manufacturers , have allowed drivers to illegally reset their hours-of-service status and drive beyond legal limits. This artificially boosted market capacity by putting vehicles on the road that shouldn't legally be there. The FMCSA is now decertifying many of these fraudulent ELD devices, which removes this artificial capacity from the market and reflects real supply tightening.

The scale of ELD manufacturing in the trucking industry creates a compliance blind spot. When so many vendors self-certify their own devices rather than undergoing independent verification, the door opens for designs that subtly or overtly allow drivers to manipulate their hours-of-service records. This regulatory weakness is explored in depth in the episode , where capacity trends and enforcement actions are analyzed together.

The connection between ELD fraud and capacity is straightforward but often overlooked. A driver using a fraudulent ELD can legally drive 11 hours per day; if that device allows them to reset their clock, they can push beyond that limit. Multiply this across thousands of vehicles, and you have phantom capacity—trucks appearing in the market that shouldn't be available under real compliance. When FMCSA decertifies these devices, it forces compliance back into the system, and that artificial capacity evaporates overnight.
Electronic Logging Device (ELD)

A device mandated by the U.S. Department of Transportation to electronically record a commercial truck driver's hours of service. Federal regulations limit drivers to 11 hours of driving per 14-hour duty period, and ELDs track compliance with this rule. Fraudulent versions can circumvent these limits.

This phenomenon is particularly significant in understanding the 2026 freight market shift. As Brett Leifert explains in the episode , the market has moved from years of excess capacity to a fundamentally tighter supply landscape. Part of that tightening is real—carrier exits, driver attrition, school closures—but part of it is enforcement removing phantom capacity that never should have existed. The FMCSA's decertification campaign is not just regulatory housekeeping; it's rebalancing the actual available supply against the legally compliant supply.

A Broken Insurance Economics Cycle

Insurers are caught in a math problem: they are paying out more in claims than they collect in premiums, even after raising rates. As Brett Leifert explains in the episode , this creates an endless loop where rate increases become the only lever insurers can pull to restore profitability . Yet because the underlying claims frequency or severity remains elevated, the gap between premiums and losses never truly closes.

Carriers absorb these rate hikes as a fixed cost component of their operating expenses. Unlike fuel or labor, which can be negotiated or offset, insurance is mandatory and largely non-negotiable. Each year's rate increase tightens carrier margins, particularly for smaller fleets with less leverage in the insurance marketplace.
The Liability Verdict Effect

The pressure doesn't stop at cargo coverage. Nuclear verdicts in liability lawsuits have exploded damages expectations , making general liability and auto liability policies far more expensive. These two cost vectors—cargo losses and verdict-driven liability claims—are hitting carriers simultaneously, compounding the effect on their bottom line.

f: The SCOTUS ruling has fundamentally altered broker-carrier dynamics by requiring stricter safety and vetting protocols for brokerages to manage their legal exposure . Carriers are no longer willing to operate under conditional relationships—the market practice of secondary or less-vetted carrier agreements is rapidly disappearing.

This shift represents a material tightening of risk management across the brokerage sector. Where brokers once maintained a tiered network of carriers with varying levels of compliance scrutiny, regulatory pressure now demands comprehensive due diligence on every carrier partner. The cost and complexity of this vetting process has become a barrier that many brokers cannot sustain.

The practical outcome is stark: brokers are losing carrier capacity they once relied on. As Brett Leifert explains in the episode , conditional carriers—the second and third-tier operators that filled capacity gaps—are simply not an option anymore. This forces brokers to compete harder for approved, fully-vetted carriers, reducing their negotiating position and access to flexible supply.

Self-certification abuse during COVID and market distortion

The COVID pandemic created conditions where CDL schools expanded rapidly by leveraging self-certification practices. These schools essentially certified their own training quality without independent verification, allowing them to operate outside traditional regulatory guardrails. This proliferation meant that training standards became inconsistent across the industry , with some operators cutting corners to maximize enrollment and revenue.

The impact rippled through the entire supply chain—carriers downstream received drivers with questionable training backgrounds, and market participants questioned the legitimacy of the CDL credential itself. As Brett Leifert explains in the episode , this enforcement action directly addressed the mismatch between claimed qualifications and actual driver competence.
FMCSA enforcement and supply chain consequences

FMCSA's response was decisive and large-scale. Closing over 50 schools simultaneously sent a clear signal that self-certification was no longer tolerable. The agency coordinated multi-state enforcement across major trucking hubs—Texas, California, and the Southwest—where concentration of CDL training activity was highest.

Staying proactive about these compliance steps saves time on both sides of the onboarding process and keeps your carrier profile in good standing with brokerages.

Onboarding delays often stem from incomplete or outdated documentation. As Eric Garcia explains in the Hit The Brakes episode , compliance is one of the most important priorities for both carriers and freight brokers. A lapsed or missing Certificate of Insurance is one of the fastest ways to halt an onboarding application before it even gets reviewed.

Beyond your COI, the FMCSA system must reflect your current fleet composition. Every time you add a truck or trailer, report the vehicle and its plate numbers to the FMCSA without delay . Brokerages cross-reference this data during vetting, and discrepancies between your application and official FMCSA records create immediate red flags that stall the process.

Contact information accuracy is equally critical. A point emphasized throughout the onboarding conversation , outdated phone numbers or email addresses mean brokerages cannot reach you during the vetting phase. Maintain a single, monitored communication channel so brokers can verify information quickly and move your application forward.

Three layers of identity and compliance verification

The core of Fetch Freight's protection strategy rests on transparent carrier identification. Every shipment includes specific truck and trailer plate numbers shared directly with the customer before pickup. This eliminates ambiguity: a customer knows exactly which vehicle should arrive, making it nearly impossible for an unauthorized carrier to slip through and steal the load.

Real-time tracking serves as the second layer. As explained in the episode , this constant visibility allows customers to monitor the load throughout its journey, immediately spotting any deviation or unauthorized handoff. Customers are explicitly warned not to accept pickup from anyone else, creating a fail-safe against social engineering.

The third layer is ongoing compliance monitoring . Fetch tracks carrier insurance status—specifically Certificate of Insurance (COI) expiration and FMCSA standing. The moment a carrier's insurance lapses or their compliance status changes, Fetch sends automatic alerts to customers. This prevents accidental load handoff to a carrier that no longer meets safety and liability standards, a critical gap in traditional vetting.
